title: Resolving vectors into perpendicular components
prior_knowledge_summary: A vector quantity has magnitude and direction.
Vector arrows represent magnitude by length and direction by the arrowhead.
Coplanar vectors can be added head-to-tail and subtracted by reversing the vector being subtracted.
The magnitude and direction of a resultant can be obtained from a completed right-angled vector triangle.
new_learning: A single vector can be represented by two perpendicular component vectors whose vector sum is the original vector.
A component is the projection of the original vector along a chosen axis.
When an angle is measured from an axis, the component along that axis is adjacent to the angle and the perpendicular component is opposite.
Component directions and signs must be retained when resolved vectors are later combined.
The original vector can be reconstructed from its perpendicular components as an independent check.
not_yet_taught: Applications of components that depend on later Physics topics.
Later-topic force, motion, momentum, field or energy equations.

learning_outcomes.text: represent a vector as two perpendicular components

visual_planning.reason: Six planned figures make projection, axis choice, angle reference, two complete calculation routes, signed directions and reconstruction checks visible without relying on later-topic physics.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: How much of one diagonal move is east?
content: A map instruction says to move 40 m in one diagonal direction. The arrow is clear, but a narrow east-west path and a north-south path cannot follow that diagonal directly.
We need two simpler moves that have exactly the same combined effect: one east-west move and one north-south move.
Those two perpendicular moves are the components of the original vector. Added head-to-tail, they must finish at the same point as the diagonal arrow.

figure.purpose: Create the need to replace one diagonal vector with two perpendicular moves that reach the same endpoint.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch. Show one diagonal 40 m arrow from a start point to an endpoint. Beside it, show an unlabeled horizontal-then-vertical route connecting the same two points. Add a small question mark beside each perpendicular leg. Do not include trigonometric equations or numerical component values.
figure.alt_text: A diagonal vector and a two-stage perpendicular route connect the same start and endpoint.

blocks.title: One vector, two perpendicular components
content: Choose two perpendicular axes, such as east and north. From the head of the original vector, project to each axis to form a right-angled triangle.

The horizontal arrow is the component along the east-west axis. The vertical arrow is the component along the north-south axis. Each component is itself a vector, so it needs a magnitude and direction.
The components are not extra vectors added to the situation. They are another representation of the same original vector. Adding the two components head-to-tail reconstructs the original arrow.
A different pair of perpendicular axes can give different component values, but the components on any chosen pair must still add to the same original vector.

figure.purpose: Show perpendicular components as projections whose vector sum reproduces one unchanged diagonal vector.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper vector sketch with east and north axes. Draw one green diagonal vector V from the origin. Add a blue eastward component and orange northward component as the sides of a right-angled triangle, with light projection guides from the diagonal head. Include a second small head-to-tail view showing the two components ending at the same head as V. Keep labels symbolic only.
figure.alt_text: A diagonal vector is represented by eastward and northward perpendicular components that add back to the same vector.

blocks.title: Let the angle decide sine or cosine
content: Do not memorise that horizontal always means cosine. First mark the stated angle on the right-angled component triangle.

If a vector of magnitude V makes angle $\theta$ with the horizontal axis, the horizontal component is adjacent to $\theta$, so its magnitude is $V\cos\theta$. The vertical component is opposite, so its magnitude is $V\sin\theta$.
If the same angle is measured from the vertical axis, the vertical component is now adjacent and uses $V\cos\theta$. The horizontal component is opposite and uses $V\sin\theta$.
The words adjacent and opposite are safer than assigning one trigonometric function permanently to one direction. Attach the original vector's unit to both components.

figure.purpose: Compare angle measured from horizontal with angle measured from vertical so sine and cosine follow the triangle rather than a memorised axis rule.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-panel comparison. Both panels show the same diagonal vector and perpendicular component triangle. In the left panel mark theta from horizontal and label adjacent V cos theta, opposite V sin theta. In the right panel mark the complementary angle from vertical and show that adjacent and opposite swap axes. Use the same colours for corresponding components.
figure.alt_text: The component beside the stated angle uses cosine and the component opposite the angle uses sine.

blocks.title: Resolve an angle measured from east
content: Consider a displacement of 52 m at $32^\circ$ north of east. Draw east and north axes, place the 32 degree angle next to the east axis and make the displacement the hypotenuse.
The east component is adjacent: $s_E=52\cos32^\circ=44.0985\ldots\,\mathrm{m}$, so $s_E=44\,\mathrm{m}$ to two significant figures.
The north component is opposite: $s_N=52\sin32^\circ=27.5558\ldots\,\mathrm{m}$, so $s_N=28\,\mathrm{m}$ to two significant figures.
A second explanation uses projections: drop a vertical line from the head of the 52 m arrow. Its horizontal shadow is the east component and its vertical rise is the north component.
Independent check: $\sqrt{44.0985^2+27.5558^2}=52.0000\,\mathrm{m}$ and $\tan^{-1}(27.5558/44.0985)=32.0000^\circ$. The components reconstruct both the magnitude and direction.

figure.purpose: Model a complete component-resolution sequence for an angle measured from the horizontal, including units, rounding and an independent reconstruction check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated worked layout. Show a 52 m vector at 32 degrees north of east, the component triangle, adjacent and opposite labels, substitution lines, rounded east and north results, and a small reconstruction check using Pythagoras and inverse tangent. Use generous spacing and a limited colour palette.
figure.alt_text: A 52 metre vector at 32 degrees north of east resolves into about 44 metres east and 28 metres north.

blocks.title: Resolve an angle measured from north
content: Now consider a 64 N vector at $25^\circ$ east of north. The angle is beside the north axis, so the north component is adjacent and the east component is opposite.
The north component is $F_N=64\cos25^\circ=58.0037\ldots\,\mathrm{N}$, so $F_N=58\,\mathrm{N}$ to two significant figures.
The east component is $F_E=64\sin25^\circ=27.0476\ldots\,\mathrm{N}$, so $F_E=27\,\mathrm{N}$ to two significant figures.
A second route uses the complementary angle. The vector is $65^\circ$ above east, so $64\cos65^\circ$ gives the east component and $64\sin65^\circ$ gives the north component. The same values return.
Independent check: $\sqrt{58.0037^2+27.0476^2}=64.0000\,\mathrm{N}$. Each component is smaller than the original magnitude, as expected for a vector between the two positive axes.

figure.purpose: Demonstrate that an angle measured from the vertical changes which component is adjacent, while a complementary-angle route confirms the result.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked comparison. Main triangle shows 64 N at 25 degrees east of north, with north adjacent and east opposite. A smaller side panel marks the complementary 65 degree angle from east and displays the alternative sine and cosine expressions. Include the 58 N north and 27 N east results and the Pythagoras check.
figure.alt_text: A 64 newton vector at 25 degrees east of north resolves into about 58 newtons north and 27 newtons east.

blocks.title: Keep directions, then add matching components
content: Trigonometry gives component magnitudes. The diagram gives their directions and, if signed axes are used, their signs.

Take east and north as positive. A 70 m vector at $40^\circ$ south of west has a west component of $70\cos40^\circ=53.6231\ldots\,\mathrm{m}$ and a south component of $70\sin40^\circ=44.9951\ldots\,\mathrm{m}$.
As directed components, report 54 m west and 45 m south. As signed components on east-north axes, report $s_E=-54\,\mathrm{m}$ and $s_N=-45\,\mathrm{m}$.
The sign is not created by sine or cosine. It comes from the component arrow pointing opposite to the chosen positive axis.

Now add a separate 18 m east vector. It contributes $+18\,\mathrm{m}$ east and zero north. Add only matching axes: the final components are $-53.6231+18=-35.6231\,\mathrm{m}$ east-axis and $-44.9951+0=-44.9951\,\mathrm{m}$ north-axis.
Reconstruct the combined vector: $R=\sqrt{35.6231^2+44.9951^2}=57.3896\,\mathrm{m}$ and $\theta=\tan^{-1}(44.9951/35.6231)=51.6310^\circ$ south of west. Report 57.4 m at $51.6^\circ$ south of west.
Independent check: both final signed components remain negative, so the combined vector must point southwest. The reported direction does.

figure.purpose: Connect compass directions to signed components, then model a complete component-addition and reconstruction route without introducing a later-topic law.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked sequence. First show east and north positive axes with a 70 m vector 40 degrees south of west and its two negative components. Next add a separate 18 m east arrow in a component table. Finish with the new southwest component triangle, 57.4 m resultant and 51.6 degree direction check. Use arrows and colour to keep the two axes distinct.
figure.alt_text: A southwest vector is resolved into negative components, combined with an eastward vector and reconstructed as a new southwest resultant.

blocks.title: Components are not pieces cut from the arrow
content: It can feel as though the original magnitude should be divided between the two components so that their magnitudes add to the original. That treats vectors like ordinary scalar pieces.
The components are perpendicular sides of a right-angled triangle, while the original vector is the hypotenuse. Their squares, not their magnitudes, combine through Pythagoras.

A second common error is to use cosine for every horizontal component. Cosine follows the side adjacent to the stated angle. If the angle is measured from vertical, the vertical component uses cosine.
Always sketch the triangle, mark the angle, label adjacent and opposite, calculate with units, attach directions or signs, then reconstruct the vector as a check.

blocks.title: The complete Topic 1 vector route
content: To resolve a vector, choose perpendicular axes, draw the right-angled component triangle and mark exactly where the angle is measured from.
Use cosine for the adjacent component and sine for the opposite component. Keep the original unit, then attach the correct direction or sign to each component.
Check by adding the components head-to-tail. Pythagoras should recover the original magnitude and inverse tangent should recover its direction.

Topic 1 now supplies a complete foundation: physical quantities and estimates, SI unit handling, measurement quality and uncertainty, and scalar-vector reasoning including addition, subtraction and perpendicular resolution. Later Physics topics may use this toolkit, but their own physical laws have not been taught here.
